top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B011) credits one precise, general mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and turn small shocks into large, persistent fluctuations. The credit comes from a single two-author 1997 paper, so no line has to be drawn through a diffuse literature. The mechanism has been reused as a building block for nearly three decades. The citation can be limited to the collateral-price feedback, leaving out the bank-run work recognised in 2022 and the net-worth accelerator strand. The main weaknesses are that the channel is identified indirectly, so the citation should credit the mechanism and not a measured magnitude, and that Gertler and Gilchrist are left out. I rank P002 (Helpman and Melitz, B005) a close second. Its selection and reallocation margins have been tested more directly on firm-level data. Its attribution is harder to draw, because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited and Helpman's marginal credit has to be separated from Krugman's 2008 prize and from his separate B020 entry. The two are close on merit, and this ranking reflects how I weigh attribution against directness of testing. I do not use the number of supporters as evidence. P003 (B014) is a mature, well-replicated labour contribution, but it may combine two achievements under a three-name cap, and the task-framework credit partly sits outside the named laureates. I still rank it above no award because the underlying work is substantial.
recusal_note: No tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Hanson or Katz is apparent from the profile. I disclose frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell (secretary, a P001 supporter) and co-authorship with Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg (both P002 supporters). My field of macroeconomics is adjacent to the macro-finance work in P001. I am also chair. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
